intro: This guide takes your group through Elisabeth Elliot (For Teens) in thirteen weeks, one chapter a week. It’s written for teens aged about 13 to 18 and works well for a youth group, a homeschool or a small group. It follows Betty Howard from a praying home in New Jersey to the forests of Ecuador, through the deaths of her husband Jim and four other men, her years living among the Waorani, and a long life of writing and speaking about trusting God without explanations. It tells her story honestly, with her faults and hard questions left in.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand (5–10 minutes). Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (10–15 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Then close in prayer (2–3 minutes), in your own words or by turning the chapter’s closing “One thing to do this week” into a prayer together, and leave that challenge with the group for the week ahead.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself first and look over the activity; most weeks need only paper and pens, or nothing at all. This book deals with violent death, grief and widowhood, forgiveness, conflict between Christians, a marriage marked by temper and control, and dementia. Some in your group may be grieving, or living with fear or control at home, so keep personal reflection private and never press anyone to share. Make clear, as the book does, that forgiving someone is not the same as staying where they can hurt you, and be ready to follow up gently and point anyone who is struggling to a parent, pastor or other trusted adult.

weeks.summary: Betty Howard grows up one of six children in a strict, missionary-minded family that sings hymns and prays twice a day, and learns contentment in the lean years of the Great Depression. At boarding school a formidable headmistress tells the painfully shy girl that shyness is a way of being wrapped up in yourself, and Betty learns to look outward; there she also discovers Amy Carmichael and resolves to translate the Bible. The big idea: whatever your family gave you, God can give you his words, and looking outward is something you can practise.

memory_verse.text: The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, I have a beautiful inheritance.

activity.title: One Real Question
steps: Pair everyone with someone they don’t usually talk to.
Give each pair three minutes to ask each other one real question, such as “What’s something you’re looking forward to?”, and to listen properly to the answer.
Swap partners and do it once more.
Come back together and ask: what made it awkward, and what made it easier?
Discuss what Mrs DuBose meant when she said a Christian has a duty to look outward.

weeks.summary: At Wheaton Betty studies Greek to prepare for Bible translation and meets Jim Elliot, her brother’s friend, who isn’t sure whether God is calling him to stay single. In June 1948, by a cemetery, they tell each other what they feel and agree to give their love back to God, as Abraham offered Isaac, with no engagement and no promise. The big idea: a living sacrifice is not one dramatic moment but a place we keep coming back to, caring deeply and still saying to God, “It’s yours.”

memory_verse.text: I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship.

activity.title: Open Hands
steps: Ask everyone to make a tight fist, then slowly open their hand palm up, and talk about the difference between gripping something and offering it.
Have each person write down privately the one thing they want most right now.
Discuss: does trusting God with something mean pretending you don’t care about it? What did Betty and Jim actually do?
Invite everyone to pray silently over what they wrote, with open hands.
Encourage them to pray the same way each day this week.

weeks.summary: Betty studies at a strict Bible school in snowy Alberta, while Jim becomes sure God is sending him to Ecuador and sails with Pete Fleming in 1952; for four years their letters are careful and their meetings few. She trains in linguistics and sails for Ecuador as a single missionary with no promise or engagement, ready to stay single if Jim decides to. The big idea: quiet waiting isn’t doing nothing, but refusing to grab what God hasn’t given while doing today’s work well.

memory_verse.text: It is good that one should wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD.

activity.title: The Waiting Room
steps: As a group, list things teenagers wait for: results, replies, being noticed, being old enough.
Talk about what bad waiting looks like, such as constant checking, worrying or forcing things, and what good waiting looks like.
Have each person write down privately one thing they are waiting for.
Under it, have them list two useful jobs that belong to today.
Challenge everyone to do one of those jobs each time they catch themselves worrying this week.

weeks.summary: Among the Tsáchila, whom the Spanish called the Colorados, Betty starts putting an unwritten language on paper, but a young mother she is helping dies in childbirth, her language helper Don Macario is shot dead, and her suitcase of notes is stolen. Years later she wrote that the question she had to answer was not “Why did God do this?” but “Will I keep trusting him without an explanation?” The big idea: faith that trusts God only when things succeed isn’t really faith yet.

memory_verse.text: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts.

activity.title: Why or Will?
steps: Write two questions at the top of a sheet: “Why did God do this?” and “Will I keep trusting him without an explanation?”
Ask the group how each question shapes what a person does next.
Talk about the three losses in this chapter, and which one they think would have been hardest to accept.
Have each person write privately about a time they did their best and it still fell apart, adding one honest sentence to God about it.
Read Isaiah 55:8–9 together to close.

weeks.summary: Jim proposes in January 1953 on condition that Betty first learns Quichua, which she does quickly, and they marry quietly at a registry office in Quito that October. They live in a tent and then at Shandia, where Jim preaches and Betty writes the language down, and their daughter Valerie is born. The big idea: God puts people with different gifts side by side on purpose.

memory_verse.text: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil.

activity.title: Two Are Better
activity.materials: Paper, pens and a few simple patterns of shapes drawn in advance
steps: Put everyone in pairs, sitting back to back.
Give one person a pattern to describe while the other, without seeing it, tries to draw it from the description.
Swap roles with a new pattern, then compare the drawings with the originals.
Ask: what did each role need that the other didn’t have?
Talk about how Jim’s gift for speaking Quichua and Betty’s gift for writing it down worked together, and have each person think of someone whose gifts differ from theirs to thank this week.

weeks.summary: Five missionaries, Jim among them, try to reach the Waorani by lowering gifts from Nate Saint’s plane, then land on a sandbar on the Curaray River, where three Waorani visit them on the Friday. On Sunday 8 January 1956, acting partly on a lie Nenkiwi told, a group of Waorani men spear all five, who had agreed beforehand not to use their guns against them. The big idea: Jesus said a grain of wheat must die to bear fruit, and real stories hold courage, mistakes and hope together.

memory_verse.text: Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.

activity.title: What Can’t You Keep?
steps: Read Jim’s journal sentence aloud: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.”
As a group, make two lists: things nobody can keep forever, and things that can never be lost.
Discuss why the chapter says the sentence is not a plan for dying but a decision about what to hold loosely.
Have each person write privately one thing they grip too tightly, and one way to loosen their grip on it this week.

weeks.summary: Searchers find four of the men’s bodies and bury them by the beach while the five widows wait at Shell Mera. Elisabeth grieves deeply but does not decide that God has failed her; at twenty-nine, with ten-month-old Valerie, she goes back to Shandia to do the next thing, and writes Through Gates of Splendor. The big idea: strong Christians do grieve, and God is with us in our grief as we do the next thing.

memory_verse.text: Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation.

activity.title: Do the Next Thing
steps: Read the old refrain Elisabeth loved, “Doe the nexte thynge,” and ask what it means.
Talk about the idea that strong Christians don’t grieve, and why Elisabeth spent years correcting it.
Have each person think of something that feels overwhelming right now and write down, for themselves only, the very next small step.
Remind the group who they can talk to if grief or heaviness won’t lift: a parent, pastor, teacher, doctor or crisis line.

weeks.summary: The way to the Waorani opens through three Waorani women: Dayuma, who fled years before, and Mankamu and Mintaka, who walk out of the forest in 1957, Mintaka being the older woman who had stood on the sandbar with the five men. Elisabeth takes the two women into her home for about ten months and learns their language from them, and in 1958 the three return to their people and come back with an invitation. The big idea: God leads people by ways they do not know, often through ordinary kindness.

memory_verse.text: And I will lead the blind in a way that they do not know, in paths that they have not known I will guide them. I will turn the darkness before them into light, the rough places into level ground. These are the things I do, and I do not forsake them.

activity.title: Say My Name
steps: Go round the group and have each person say their full name and how they like it said, with everyone repeating it back.
Talk about how it feels when someone gets your name wrong, or never bothers to learn it.
Discuss: how did living with Mankamu and Mintaka stop Elisabeth seeing the Waorani as either noble innocents or monsters?
Have each person think of someone new or on the outside, and decide on one way to spend real time with them this week.

weeks.summary: Against her friends’ fears, Elisabeth, three-year-old Valerie and Rachel Saint walk into Waorani country in October 1958 and live in a clearing by the Tiwaeno, where Elisabeth is named Gikari, “woodpecker.” Most of the men who killed Jim, including Gikita and Mincaye, live a few yards away; she finds them ordinary people and had settled before she came that she would not hate them. The big idea: God calls us to overcome evil with good, and forgiving someone is not the same as putting yourself where they can still hurt you.

memory_verse.text: Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

activity.title: What Forgiveness Is and Isn’t
steps: Draw two columns headed “Forgiveness is” and “Forgiveness isn’t.”
As a group, fill them in: for example, it isn’t pretending a wrong didn’t matter, and it isn’t staying where someone can keep harming you.
Discuss why Elisabeth said she went as a missionary to a people, not to make a dramatic act of forgiveness.
Have each person privately write the initials of someone they hold a grudge against, and commit to pray for their good each day this week.
Remind everyone that if someone is still harming them, telling a safe adult is the right first step.

weeks.summary: Elisabeth lives about three years among the Waorani, and several people, including some of the men from the beach, begin to call themselves followers of God, while revenge killings slow among those living nearby. But she and Rachel Saint clash over personality, method and translation, and in 1961 she leaves without public complaint, returning to the United States in 1963. The big idea: God carries his treasure in breakable clay jars, so that the power is clearly his, even when Christians fail each other.

memory_verse.text: But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.

activity.title: Both Sides
steps: Split the group in two: one half lists what made Rachel hard to work with, the other what made Elisabeth hard to work with, using only the chapter.
Then have each half list what was good and devoted in the other woman.
Discuss why the chapter says neither woman comes out of it simply right.
Have each person think privately about a conflict they are in and write down one way they have made it worse.
Invite them to choose one step to put their own part right this week.

weeks.summary: Back in America Elisabeth speaks and writes, but refuses to tell the 1956 story with a neat shape, and her novel No Graven Image dismays readers by insisting that God need not produce the results we plan. She marries Addison Leitch in 1969, and in 1973 nurses him through cancer until he dies, leaving her a widow for the second time. The big idea: God is a refuge, so honest questions belong in prayer rather than hidden away.

memory_verse.text: Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us.

activity.title: Neat Story, True Story
steps: Ask the group to tell a well-known story in one tidy sentence, such as a famous sporting comeback, then add the messy details the tidy version leaves out.
Discuss why Elisabeth refused to let the story of 1956 keep its neat shape.
Talk about the title No Graven Image: how can we turn God into an idol who must give us the results we want?
Give everyone a few minutes to write, privately, an honest prayer about a question they have been hiding, ending with one sentence of trust.

weeks.summary: Elisabeth marries Lars Gren in 1977, writes Let Me Be a Woman and Passion and Purity, and for thirteen years presents the radio programme Gateway to Joy, opening every day with God’s everlasting love. Her authorised biographer reports that at home Lars was given to outbursts of temper and came to control much of her life, something she never spoke of in public. The big idea: God’s everlasting love meets us in small daily duties, and a hidden burden at home is worth telling a safe person about.

memory_verse.text: I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you.

activity.title: Small Things
steps: As a group, list small, unnoticed duties in an ordinary week: dishes, replying to a message, tidying a room, being on time.
Discuss why Elisabeth believed doing small duties faithfully is not a lesser kind of devotion than dramatic sacrifice.
Have each person choose one small duty to do this week without being asked, and write it down for themselves.
Close by repeating the chapter’s reminder: if someone at home frightens or controls you, tell a safe person such as a pastor, teacher, doctor or helpline.

weeks.summary: In 1996 Elisabeth adds an epilogue admitting the Waorani story was more tangled than first told; soon afterwards dementia takes away her words, and Lars cares for her at home for most of fifteen years until she dies in 2015. Mincaye, one of the men from the beach, becomes a close friend of Nate Saint’s son Steve and travels with him telling his story. The big idea: God carries his people all the way to grey hair, and a life that can do almost nothing is still precious to him.

memory_verse.text: Even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save.

activity.title: Carried
steps: Ask the group to list the people Elisabeth carried through her life, and the people who carried her at the end.
Discuss: what makes a person valuable, if it isn’t what they can do?
Have each person write the name of an elderly person they could visit, call or write to this week.
Look back over the thirteen weeks and invite each person to share one thing from Elisabeth’s life they want to remember.
